title: Game Twelve, First Half
part: PART FOUR: THE OTHER KIND OF CONFIDENCE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #49: Let somebody else's dad tell you who you are.*

Saturday morning arrives with humidity that makes the grass smell like wet socks and ambition. Marigold Park is packed.

My dad holds his foam finger high enough to block the sun for a small flock of confused sparrows. Abuela sits in her folding chair, fanning herself with a newspaper. She looks ready to argue with the referee about offside, which she still thinks is a moral failing.

Luz is beside her, a fresh crayon notebook in her lap. The title page says DEPUTY WIN LOG in bright purple. She is optimistic. She is dangerous.

Carter Boyle is on the bleachers. He has his phone out, but he does not turn it on. He just watches. It is a small, quiet revolution.

The Northgate Wolves are in their black and white kits, looking polished and expensive. Their coach, Mr. Brandt, looks like he has never lost a game, a bet, or an argument.

He is shouting at his striker before the whistle has even blown. Kai Brandt nods. He is not arrogant. He is focused.

The ducks gather at the edge of the pond to watch and wait. They know exactly what happens here.
pages.image: A crowded muddy soccer field sideline with a large man in a mechanic shirt waving a yellow foam finger, a small woman fanning herself with a newspaper, and a young girl writing in a purple notebook; black and white jerseys visible on the field.

pages.text:
The whistle blows, and the Wolves move. They don't run; they glide. The ball slides between their feet with a smoothness that makes my stomach turn over like a spilled carton of juice. By the third possession, they have it in the box.

Kai Brandt takes the shot. It is low, fast, and perfect.

Priya sees it come. I watch her eyes track the angle, her tiny body shifting. Her glove touches the ball. It changes direction, but not enough. The ball kisses the back of the net. One to zero.

Coach Brandt slams his hand against his thigh. He doesn't yell. He roars. It sounds like a heavy metal door being forced open.

My stomach drops. The old empty feeling rushes in. The feeling that I am nothing.

Then I feel the card in my sock. It is heavy. It is warm. It is mine.

I am still here. I am still Dani. The score is one. I am zero. But I am still here.
pages.image: A tiny girl in a goalkeeper uniform with oversized gloves reaching for a soccer ball near the net while a tall coach in a black suit shouts angrily on the sideline; a small duck watches from the water's edge.

pages.text:
We do not panic. We do the thing Coach Gin taught us, which is to stop staring at the scoreboard and start looking at the grass.

Ahmed has the ball. He is fast, always fast, but this time he holds it. He sees the twins. Leo signals. Mateo nods. Josie is already shouting, "Space! Left side! Ahmed, LEFT!"

Ahmed does not run straight. He cuts. He passes to Josie, who flicks it to the twins, and they thread it to me.

I have the ball. I see the gap. Two Wolves defenders are coming. I do not kick it hard. I thread it. I put my toe on the top of the ball and I lift it just enough to go over their heads and into the feet of Ahmed, who is already running.

He shoots. It goes in.

One to one.

The park explodes. My dad is screaming. Abuela is standing up. Luz is writing GOAL in giant red letters.

And I am not screaming. I am not jumping. I am just standing there, breathing. My hands are steady. The ball went where I wanted it to go. That is enough.
pages.image: A muddy soccer field with players in red jerseys celebrating a goal; a girl with a high ponytail and yellow armband stands calmly in the center while a large boy runs toward the net; a crowd cheers in the background.

pages.text:
The Wolves reset, and the air in the park gets heavy. Kai Brandt wants the ball, and he comes down the wing with a purpose that feels like a math test I didn't study for. Tank is there, waiting.

Tank is twelve, the size of a refrigerator, and the gentlest person I know. Kai goes for a dribble, but Tank does not lunge or flail. He simply steps in and puts his body in the way, like a door closing on a draft. It is a perfect, clean tackle. The ball pops loose, and Kai goes down.

Tank stands over him. He does not say sorry.

Kai looks up from the grass. He is staring at Tank, and then he grins. It is a real grin, not the fake one he wears on the scoreboard. He looks at Tank, and then he looks at the crowd.

Tank offers a hand. "Sorry," he says. "For not apologizing sooner."

The whole park laughs. Even Coach Brandt stops shouting for a second to check his watch. Coach Gin sips her tea. She does not say a word. She does not need to.
pages.image: A large, gentle boy in a red jersey offering a hand to a fallen player in a black and white uniform; the fallen player is smiling up at him; a small girl in goalkeeper gear watches nearby.

pages.text:
The whistle blows, sharp and final, signaling the end of the first half.

One to one.

Northgate has not been level at half-time all season. Their coach, Coach Brandt, is in the far corner, lecturing his team with frantic hand gestures. He is drawing imaginary diagrams in the air, his face a mask of pure, undiluted anger. He looks like a teacher whose whiteboard was just erased by a student.

On our side, it is quiet.

Coach Gin walks over to Ollie, who is standing by the bench holding his bag of orange slices. He has brought hundreds, probably a thousand, and he looks like he is waiting to serve a banquet at a royal wedding.

Gin takes a slice. She eats it in one bite. She looks at us.

"You're doing it," she says, her voice calm as the lake behind the park. "Now the hard part."

She gestures to the scoreboard. It glows red. One to one.

"Don't do anything different because of the score," she says.

I look at the board. It has been showing one to one for ten minutes. My hands are steady. My heart is beating, but it is a good beat, a steady beat, like the metronome in music class.

I am ready for the second half.
pages.image: A soccer coach in a yellow windbreaker eating an orange slice while looking at a group of young players in red jerseys; a scoreboard with only small round lights in the background shows the number one on both sides.
